cards.title: Why Cold AI Hooks Fail (and the Copy-Paste Fallback Also Fails)
cards.summary: Generic LLM hook output is bland because the model isn't grounded in short-form social data, and cloning viral hooks across niches breaks on psychology, format and grammar.
cards.use_when: You are briefing AI (or a copywriter) to write paid-ad or organic video hooks for your store and wondering why output feels generic, or considering lifting a competitor's viral hook verbatim.
steps: Recognize the two default failure modes before you spend creative budget on them: (1) dumping a product benefit into a cold chat and asking 'write me hooks' produces generic, non-compelling copy because the model isn't calibrated on short-form social data without extensive training; (2) taking a hook that went viral in another niche and pasting it into yours usually underperforms because the psychology doesn't translate, the format crossover is mismatched, and the grammar doesn't fit.
Treat both as symptoms of having no grounding data, not as reasons to give up on AI.
Replace the cold prompt with a data-grounded pipeline: feed the model real transcripts and performance metrics from hooks that actually worked, then let it derive principles rather than invent copy.

For ecommerce, run this on your own top-performing ad creative and organic videos (and close competitor creative in the same style) so extracted principles match your product's buying psychology, not another category's.
Expect the output to be candidate hooks that a human filters and edits — the source presents the AI as producing graded options and rewrites, not final copy.
caveats: The 'billion views / thousands of videos studied' credentials are the presenter's promotional framing, not evidence your niche will behave the same way.
Cross-niche copying sometimes works; the source claims it usually fails, which is a practitioner's opinion.

cards.title: The Four-Step Hook Machine Workflow
cards.summary: A four-step AI workflow — connect a data source, scrape top videos, sort winners from losers, extract psychological and grammatical rules — that yields a custom hook grading rubric and generator.
cards.use_when: You want a repeatable system for producing and grading short-form hooks for product ads or content, instead of writing each hook from scratch.
steps: Step 1 — Get a data source with an MCP: the source requires a Sandcastles account (at least Pro) plus the Claude Desktop app, because the MCP is the pipe that lets Claude pull social video metrics and transcripts. Without the pipe, no deep analysis is possible. Verify current setup instructions and product tiers before relying on any specific plan.
Step 2 — Connect the MCP to Claude Desktop once (the source links a roughly two-minute setup walkthrough). Desktop app is required to run the cowork/code environment.
Step 3 — Paste the provided prompt, supply your channel plus competitor channels, and let it scrape the top 10 videos per channel. Tell it to ignore off-topic (personal-life) videos.

Step 4 — Let it sort top videos into winners and losers, extract per-channel psychology, trigger-word, grammatical and non-obvious takeaways, synthesize cross-channel patterns, then build a rubric and library of winning hooks.
Finish by feeding in a new topic or a draft hook so it grades against the rubric (e.g. a 'B') and rewrites.
Keep the project saved in cowork so you can reuse the rubric and generator for later topics without rerunning the full scrape.
caveats: Credit and processing costs scale with videos analyzed; analyzing already-processed videos is cheaper than fresh scrapes.
Named tools and the exact prompt are specific to this presenter's stack and may change — verify the interface before building it into a workflow.

cards.title: Filter Brand Deals Out of Hook Analysis With a 2% Engagement Floor
cards.summary: Screen out any video below roughly 2% engagement before analyzing hooks, because paid spend inflates view counts and corrupts the winner data.
cards.use_when: You are assembling a set of top-performing competitor or own-brand videos to extract hook and creative principles from.
steps: When building the analysis set, explicitly instruct the tool to screen out paid brand deals.
Apply the source's default rule of thumb: any high-view video with below roughly 2% engagement rate is likely paid spend artificially inflating its performance.
Exclude those videos rather than studying their hooks as if they were organic winners.
Confirm the filter in the run — the source shows the tool flagging a competitor video at approximately 0% engagement as clearly paid and removing it.
Re-run the filter any time you refresh the source channel list, since new sponsored posts will appear.
caveats: 2% is the source's heuristic, not a derived benchmark; engagement norms vary by platform and account size, so sanity-check before relying on it.
Some genuinely strong organic videos may sit near the threshold and get removed; you can override the line if a known organic winner is excluded.

cards.title: Find the View Drop-Off Break Point to Separate Winners From Losers
cards.summary: Sort a channel's top 10 videos by views, locate the natural break point, and treat videos above it as the hook principles worth extracting.
cards.use_when: You need to decide which of your or a competitor's videos to study for ad hook and creative format patterns, and which are just baseline performers.
steps: Take the channel's top 10 videos ranked by views and look for a natural discontinuity — in the source's examples, breaks occurred between video 4 and 5, or after 4–5 videos across different channels.
Label everything above the break as winners and everything below as losers; the claim is content follows an 80/20 pattern where a few big hits drive most growth.
Keep the analysis segmented per creator rather than merging all videos into one pool, so you can see each creator's own winner/loser difference.

Review the line the tool proposes and adjust it manually if the channels are quite different in size — the source notes smaller channels may have slightly different break points but kept the defaults.
Feed only the above-the-line winners into principle extraction; use the losers as contrast cases for what to avoid.
caveats: Break-point position is subjective and channel-specific; the source says you can change it.
Small top-10 samples (four or five winners) produce thin principle sets — analyzing a whole backlog yields more.

cards.title: Extract Hook Principles in Four Buckets (Psychology, Framing, Grammar, Non-Obvious)
cards.summary: Have the analysis classify winner-vs-loser differences into psychology, trigger words and framing, grammatical structure, and non-obvious takeaways — then turn them into rules.
cards.use_when: You are converting raw video performance data into concrete creative rules for writing product ad hooks or landing-page headlines.
steps: For each creator separately, run four comparison buckets between winners and losers: (1) psychology takeaways, (2) trigger words and framing, (3) grammatical structure, (4) non-obvious takeaways.

Look for the pattern in the contrast. Example from the source's own channel: winners attach a concrete outcome to a constrained input ('30 days of content in 30 minutes'); losers lean on series branding with no standalone value promise in the first sentence.
Use the framing bucket to separate specific everyday language from vague superlatives.
Use grammar to check payoff placement — the source found declarative, front-loaded payoff hooks beat hooks that delay the takeaway.
Log each finding as a rule with its source video, as the tool does when it tags custom principles to their origin, so you can trace why a rewrite changed.
caveats: This only works on transcripts and visual analysis, not captions or view counts alone — surface-level scrapers won't produce it.
With few videos the rules are provisional; the source says results shift with more videos or different channels.

cards.title: Don't Cross-Pollinate Creator Styles in One Analysis
cards.summary: Mashing multiple creators with different styles into a single analysis dilutes extracted hook principles toward an ineffective average.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to run one hook-extraction pass across several competitor accounts or separate passes per account.
steps: Recognize that combining distinct creator styles — a concise tight speaker versus a long-winded 'yapper' — averages their hook rules into something that fits nobody.
Prefer running the flow separately per creator so each generates a creator-specific hook generator (e.g. a 'Brier hook writer', a 'bonus-footage hook writer').
If you do run a multi-channel pass, read the cross-channel synthesis only for genuinely shared principles, and treat divergences as divergence rather than evidence one is wrong.

When generating hooks for your own store's ads, filter the generated set by whether the source format fits the topic — the source shows stat/case-study formats being ruled out for a conceptual topic and the model correctly skipping incompatible templates.
Reject any generated hook whose style doesn't match your brand voice, even if it scored well on the rubric.
caveats: The dilution warning is the presenter's hypothesis ('I have a feeling'), supported by observed friction when merging styles, not a tested benchmark.
Cross-channel synthesis is still useful when competitors genuinely share a format.

cards.title: Build a Custom Hook Rubric From Data, Then Grade and Rewrite Draft Hooks
cards.summary: Combine a fixed set of universal storytelling principles with principles extracted from your data, then grade any new hook against that rubric and generate rewrites.
cards.use_when: You have drafted a hook for an ad or video and want a structured critique plus concrete alternative versions before spending on creative.
steps: Build the rubric in two parts: universal hook principles (the source uses eight) plus custom principles tagged to the specific videos they came from (the source yielded eleven in its demo run).

Feed in a draft hook as plain text. In the source's example: 'This is how you get people actually addicted to your content. It's called dopamine ladders. And once you learn it, you'll never look at content the same way again.'

Read the line-by-line breakdown, not just the letter grade. It scored a B, with critique that the distillation was weak, the phrase 'this is how you' was soft with no specificity, and credibility anchoring was absent.
Use the rewrite suggestions to see the specific fixes: one rewrite added a concrete number ('there are exactly six rungs'), another replaced a vague claim with a comparative mechanism.
Pick the rewrite that fits your topic and voice; the source's own preference among rewrites was for the one with a concrete comparative structure.
Save the rubric as a reusable project so repeated hook drafts can be graded without rerunning the full scrape.
caveats: Grades are only as good as the rubric, which is built from a small sample and will change with different source channels or larger video sets.
Letter grades reflect the presenter's own coded criteria and are not an external standard.

cards.title: Analyze Your Own Backlog First — Competitors Second
cards.summary: The strongest hook rubric comes from running the system on your own videos, then adding competitors one at a time rather than in a single mixed batch.
cards.use_when: You are setting up a long-term hook or ad-copy generation system for your store's content channels.
steps: Start by analyzing your own channel's backlog so the extracted principles reflect your voice and audience, not someone else's.
Analyze a large set — the source suggests around 100 own videos, running the top ~20 through the process and letting the break point fall naturally (likely around 10–15 winners).
Keep your own-channel analysis as its own generator, since the source notes originals are only built on the storyteller's principles plus your account, not competitors'.
Add competitors afterwards, one per analysis run, so each produces a distinct generator rather than an averaged one.
Re-run the rubric periodically with fresh or expanded data — the source says the rubric changes with different video sets, so it is not one-and-done.
Use the bonus hook format library (original hook plus its format/Mad-Lib) exported from winning videos as a reusable swipe file for future creative briefs.
caveats: Cost scales with videos analyzed; analyzing 100 videos at roughly one credit each is a real spend, though already-processed videos don't double-charge.
You can drop transcripts in manually to avoid per-video analysis credits, but you lose the visual and metric analysis the tool performs.

cards.title: Use Topic-Format Compatibility Screening Before Generating Hooks
cards.summary: Before generating hooks, filter winning formats by whether they fit the topic — forcing a stat/case-study template onto a conceptual topic reproduces the cross-pollination failure.
cards.use_when: You are generating ad hooks or video hooks for a specific product or concept and have a library of proven competitor formats available.
steps: Establish the nature of the topic first — is it a data/stat claim, a case study, or a conceptual framework?
Screen the format library against that nature: the source shows a stat/case-study style library failing compatibility for a conceptual 'dopamine ladders' topic, with four of five formats rejected.
Accept that rejection as correct behavior, not a failure — it prevents the format cross-pollination the source warns against.
Generate only from compatible formats, and let the tool produce up to about five hooks per creator, limited by how many winning formats actually matched.
Treat the set of compatible formats as a natural cap on output; if too few formats fit, the answer is to analyze more videos, not to force-fit templates.
caveats: With a small analyzed set the compatible format pool can be tiny (the source got roughly seven to nine usable hooks across all sources).
Compatibility judgement is made by the model and should be sanity-checked against your knowledge of your audience.

cards.title: Prefer Transcript-Based Analysis Over Lightweight Caption Scraping
cards.summary: Deep hook extraction depends on transcripts, visual layout and metrics — lightweight scraper connections only surface captions and rankings and miss the principles.
cards.use_when: You are choosing tooling to research creative for your store's ads and deciding how deep the analysis needs to go.
steps: Distinguish two levels of tooling: lightweight API connections that pull metrics and captions (good only for ranking which videos did best) versus an analysis layer that processes the transcript, ideas, topic, hook format, storytelling format, and visual layout.

Only the deeper layer can surface non-obvious findings — the source's example being that audio-clip openers underperformed by roughly 60% for one creator, which requires transcript and visual analysis to detect.
When budget is tight, do the scraping and ranking yourself, and spend on the deep analysis of a smaller, well-chosen winner set.
Alternative workflow the source describes: run bulk analysis in the source tool's web app (faster than through the data pipe) and export the results as CSV to drop into the analysis.
Choose the pipeline based on whether the decision you're making needs rankings only or extracted copy principles.
caveats: The 'free unlimited scraping' framing is the presenter's product positioning; verify current pricing and tiers.
Specific tool names, credit rates and MCP tool counts (the source mentions around 24 tools) can change — check the current interface.
